articles.title: Brave Enough to Be the Dawn
articles.dek: To a hurting church that wondered whether it was still in the dark, the aging apostle John wrote that morning was already breaking, and that the first signs of it were showing up in them.
articles.quote: The dawn John describes is already breaking, and the clearest place it shows is in the way you love the person in front of you.
articles.body:
On a cold January morning in 2021, a twenty-two-year-old woman in a bright yellow coat and a red satin headband stepped up to a podium on the steps of the United States Capitol. Her name was Amanda Gorman, and she was about to become the youngest poet ever to read at an American presidential inauguration. Two weeks earlier, the building behind her had been overrun by a mob, and she had stayed up that night finishing the poem she now held in her hands. Millions were watching, many of them worn down by a long year of pandemic and grief.

Few of them knew that as a child Gorman had struggled with a speech impediment, and that certain sounds, especially the letter r, used to tangle on her tongue. She has said she trained herself by reciting the song "Aaron Burr, Sir" from the musical Hamilton again and again, because it was packed with the very sounds she found hardest. The girl who once dreaded speaking aloud now spoke to a nation with a voice that rose and held. Her closing lines traveled around the world within hours, reaching Filipinos still awake past midnight in Manila: "When day comes, we step out of the shade, aflame and unafraid. The new dawn blooms as we free it. For there is always light, if only we're brave enough to see it. If only we're brave enough to be it."

That final turn, from seeing the light to being it, carries an old echo. Nearly two thousand years earlier, an aging pastor wrote a letter built on the same conviction, and he wrote it to people who badly needed to hear it.

The pastor was John, the last living apostle, most likely writing from Ephesus near the end of the first century. The churches under his care had just been through a painful split. A group had walked out, and John describes it with a sigh you can almost hear: "They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us" (1 John 2:19). Those who left claimed a superior spiritual knowledge. They spoke of themselves as people of the light, and they treated the believers who stayed with quiet contempt.

Picture one of those small house churches on the evening John's letter arrives. The oil lamps are lit, and the benches have gaps where friends used to sit. Someone unrolls the scroll and begins to read aloud, and the room is tense, because everyone is privately asking the same question: if the confident ones left, are we the ones in the dark? Then the reader comes to these words: "Dear friends, I am not writing you a new command but an old one, which you have had since the beginning" (1 John 2:7). The old command was the one they had learned at their conversion, rooted as far back as Leviticus 19:18 and sharpened by Jesus himself: "Love one another. As I have loved you, so you must love one another" (John 13:34). And then John adds a sentence that must have made the lamplit room go still.

"Yet I am writing you a new command; its truth is seen in him and in you, because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining." (1 John 2:8)

The Greek word John uses for "new" is kainos, which describes something new in quality, freshly made, rather than merely recent. The command to love was ancient, yet in Jesus it had been remade, because now everyone could see what that love actually looked like: a Teacher washing feet and a Savior laying down his life. The verb for "is passing" is paragetai, and it sits in the present tense, describing something in motion. John uses the same word a few verses later: "The world and its desires pass away" (1 John 2:17). In other words, the night is still here, yet it is leaving. Anyone who has stood in a province before sunrise knows that hour, when the rooster has crowed and the sky over the rice fields is still dark, but a thin gray line along the mountains tells you the outcome is already settled.

The phrase that opens this verse most beautifully is easy to read past. John says the truth of this command "is seen in him and in you." He places those frightened, diminished believers in the same sentence as Jesus Christ. The first evidence that dawn has come is the life of Jesus, and the second evidence, John says, is them. The people who walked out claimed to have the light, but the light John recognizes looks like ordinary Christians loving one another in a half-empty room. One way to read this is that the dawn does more than shine on believers. It shines through them, so that their love becomes one of the ways the world can tell morning has arrived.

John then makes the test plain. "Anyone who claims to be in the light but hates a brother or sister is still in the darkness" (1 John 2:9). He goes on: "Anyone who loves their brother and sister lives in the light, and there is nothing in them to make them stumble" (1 John 2:10). The word behind "make them stumble" is skandalon, which originally meant the trigger stick of a trap, the small piece of wood that snaps the trap shut when an animal brushes against it. John suggests that a grudge works like a hidden trigger inside a person, waiting to spring. Love disarms it. By contrast, the one who hates "walks around in the darkness," not knowing where they are going, "because the darkness has blinded them" (1 John 2:11). Bitterness rarely announces itself as darkness. It feels like clear sight, like finally understanding who someone really is, yet John says it slowly takes away our ability to see anything at all.

This is where Gorman's line and John's letter meet. Seeing the light is a gift, and being the light takes courage. For most of us, the darkness we face this week will be close to home. It may be the tito you have not spoken to since the argument over the family land, or the officemate whose comment still stings, or the friend from church who quietly left the group chat and never came back. Each of these relationships holds a small skandalon, and every time we brush against it we feel it snap. Loving these people may mean sending the first message, offering an apology that costs us some pride, or simply speaking kindly of someone who has not spoken kindly of us.

None of this depends on our feeling bright or strong. Gorman stood on those steps carrying a childhood stammer, and the believers in Ephesus gathered carrying the wound of a split. John did not ask them to wait until the night was fully over. He told them that morning was already rising, that its proof was showing up in them, and that every act of love would add to its light. Proverbs describes the same movement: "The path of the righteous is like the morning sun, shining ever brighter till the full light of day" (Proverbs 4:18). Jesus said it more simply still: "You are the light of the world" (Matthew 5:14).

The dawn John describes is already breaking, and the clearest place it shows is in the way you love the person in front of you. Before the sun sets today, you might think of the one brother or sister whose name tightens something in your chest, and do one small, concrete thing in their direction, whether that is a prayer, a message, or a kind word to someone else about them. You do not need to fix the whole relationship by tonight. You only need to let a little more light through, because the darkness is passing, and the true light is already shining, in Christ and, by his grace, in you.

articles.title: The Hour Daniel Sat in Silence
articles.dek: Daniel had to tell the most powerful man on earth that he was about to lose everything. The way he said it is one of Scripture's wisest lessons on how to tell someone a hard truth.
articles.quote: The truth that heals is usually carried by someone who first grieved over having to say it.
articles.illustration: SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news
articles.body:
In the late 1990s, two cancer doctors, Walter Baile of the MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston and Robert Buckman of Toronto, began studying something medical training had mostly left to chance. They wanted to know how a doctor should tell a patient the worst news of that patient's life. Many physicians admitted they had never been taught. They had learned by watching older colleagues or by fumbling through it themselves, and patients often carried the bruises of those clumsy conversations for years. So Baile, Buckman and their colleagues wrote down a simple six-step guide, published in the journal The Oncologist in 2000, and gave it a name that was easy to remember: SPIKES.

The steps are humble and human. The doctor finds a quiet Setting and sits down, asks what the patient already Perceives, and waits for an Invitation to share more. Then comes the Knowledge itself, given plainly and in small pieces. After that the doctor pauses for the Emotions, naming the fear or grief out loud and staying in the room with it. Finally the doctor offers a Strategy, so that the patient walks out holding a plan along with the diagnosis. Doctors trained this way came to see that the way bad news is delivered shapes how well people understand it, how they cope, and whether they keep trusting the one who told them. People can take in hard truth when it comes with someone beside them and a way forward.

About twenty-six centuries earlier, a Jewish exile in Babylon delivered terrible news to a king in a way that looks remarkably like that guide. To feel the weight of it, we have to remember who the king was and what had just happened in his court.

Daniel 3 opens with King Nebuchadnezzar raising a golden image ninety feet high on the plain of Dura and ordering every official in the empire to bow down when the music played (Daniel 3:1–6). Three young Jewish administrators, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, would not bow. The king was “furious with rage” and ordered the furnace heated “seven times hotter than usual” (Daniel 3:19). The flames were so fierce that they killed the soldiers who threw the three men in. Then the king leaped to his feet, because he saw four men walking unbound in the fire, and the fourth looked “like a son of the gods” (Daniel 3:25). The three came out without even the smell of smoke on their clothes (Daniel 3:27).

Chapter 4 is unusual in the Bible because Nebuchadnezzar himself tells it. It is written as a royal letter “to the nations and peoples of every language, who live in all the earth” (Daniel 4:1). The king describes a dream that frightened him. He saw an enormous tree that reached the sky and fed the whole world, and then a holy messenger came down and ordered it cut to a stump, bound with iron and bronze, while the man it represented lived like an animal “until seven times pass by for him” (Daniel 4:16). The magicians and astrologers of Babylon had nothing to say. Finally Daniel came in, and he understood the dream immediately. The tree was the king.

“Then Daniel (also called Belteshazzar) was greatly perplexed for a time, and his thoughts terrified him. So the king said, ‘Belteshazzar, do not let the dream or its meaning alarm you.’ Belteshazzar answered, ‘My lord, if only the dream applied to your enemies and its meaning to your adversaries!’” (Daniel 4:19)

Consider what this man had done to Daniel. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem (Daniel 1:1), carried Daniel off to Babylon as a youth, renamed him after a Babylonian god (Daniel 1:7), and in later years burned the temple of the Lord to the ground. If anyone in that room had a reason to enjoy watching the proud king fall, it was Daniel. Instead, he was stricken. The Aramaic word translated “greatly perplexed” (eshtomam) carries the sense of being stunned or appalled, and the phrase “for a time” is literally “for one hour” (sha'ah chadah). One way to picture it is Daniel standing silent before the throne, grieving for the man who had taken everything from him, while the king, of all people, tries to comfort him.

His first words are a wish for the king's good: “if only the dream applied to your enemies.” That was probably sincere. Years earlier the prophet Jeremiah had written to the exiles in Babylon, telling them to “seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you into exile” and to pray to the Lord for it (Jeremiah 29:7). Daniel had evidently taken that letter to heart, and it reached all the way to the man on the throne.

Then Daniel told the whole truth, without softening any of it (Daniel 4:20–26). He did not trim the dream to make it easier to hear. Within that hard word, however, he pointed out the stump that would be left, a sign that the kingdom would be restored “when you acknowledge that Heaven rules” (Daniel 4:26). And he ended with a road forward: “Renounce your sins by doing what is right, and your wickedness by being kind to the oppressed. It may be that then your prosperity will continue” (Daniel 4:27). In the language of the doctors, Daniel paused for the emotion and closed with a strategy.

The king did not listen at first. Twelve months later, walking on his palace roof and admiring “the great Babylon I have built... for the glory of my majesty” (Daniel 4:30), he fell exactly as the dream had warned. But the story kept going. “At the end of that time, I, Nebuchadnezzar, raised my eyes toward heaven, and my sanity was restored” (Daniel 4:34). The whole chapter is the testimony of a humbled king, ending with his own words that God's ways are just and “those who walk in pride he is able to humble” (Daniel 4:37). This suggests that the hard word sank deep because it came from someone who plainly wished the king well. A man who had once heated a furnace seven times hotter for anyone who defied him ended up writing a letter to the whole world about his own pride.

Many of us know only two ways to handle hard truths. Some of us keep quiet to protect the peace, and the problem spreads in silence. Others of us wait until we are angry and then let the truth out hot, the way Nebuchadnezzar lit his furnace. Daniel shows a gentler way. He let the news grieve him before he said it, he spoke as someone on the other person's side, he said the whole thing clearly, and he left the door open toward home. The truth that heals is usually carried by someone who first grieved over having to say it.

You may be carrying a conversation like that right now. Perhaps it is a sibling whose drinking is hurting the family, a friend whose relationship is pulling them away from God, an aging parent who should no longer drive, or a coworker whose shortcuts will catch up with them. Before you say anything, take your own “hour” with God. Pray for that person until you can honestly say, as Daniel did, “if only this were not so for you.” Then sit down somewhere quiet, say the truth plainly and kindly, and offer one concrete next step that you are willing to walk with them.

Paul later put it in a single phrase: “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). Daniel lived that phrase in a pagan palace, to a king who had wronged him, and God used it to bring that king back to his right mind. Your words, carried with the same grief and the same hope, can be the beginning of someone's way home.

articles.title: The Child Who Asks for Nothing
articles.dek: In Psalm 131, a king who carried the weight of a nation pictures his soul as a toddler resting in its mother's lap. It is one of the gentlest invitations in all of Scripture.
articles.quote: A soul at rest has learned to come to God for God himself, and to find that he is enough.
articles.body:
In 1978, the Instituto Materno Infantil in Bogotá, Colombia, was a hospital stretched past its limits. Premature babies were arriving faster than the nursery could care for them, and there were too few incubators, so infants were sometimes placed two or three to a single machine. Infections spread easily in those conditions, and many of the smallest babies did not survive. A pediatrician named Dr. Edgar Rey Sanabria looked at the problem and reached for the one resource the hospital had in abundance. He asked mothers to hold their tiny babies upright against their bare chests, skin to skin, tucked inside their clothing, day and night.

The results surprised even the doctors. Babies held this way stayed warm on their mothers' bodies, and survival improved. Later research found more: an infant lying on a parent's chest tends to breathe more evenly, its heart rate steadies, and it settles into deeper, calmer sleep. The method came to be called kangaroo mother care, and it spread around the world, including to hospitals in the Philippines, where many a young nanay has spent long nights with a fragile newborn pressed close to her heart. What the Bogotá doctors confirmed with charts and numbers, every Filipino lola already knew by instinct. A restless child grows still against the body of the one who loves it.

Nearly three thousand years ago, a poet of Israel reached for the same image to describe what happens to a restless soul in the presence of God. Psalm 131 is one of the shortest psalms in the Bible, only three verses long, and its title reads, "A song of ascents. Of David." The Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120 to 134) were most likely sung by pilgrims as they climbed the road up to Jerusalem for the great festivals. Picture families walking for days, dusty and tired, carrying little ones on their hips and singing as they went. Somewhere on that road, they sang this small song about a child resting with its mother.

It begins with a confession of letting go. "My heart is not proud, LORD, my eyes are not haughty; I do not concern myself with great matters or things too wonderful for me" (Psalm 131:1). These are remarkable words to come from David, of all people. He was a king and a warrior, a man whose days were crowded with armies, rivals, and the future of a nation. Yet he admits there are things too wonderful for him, matters he has chosen to leave in God's hands. And then he describes what he has done with his own heart.

"But I have calmed and quieted myself, I am like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child I am content." (Psalm 131:2)

The key word is weaned. A nursing infant in its mother's arms is rarely calm for long. It roots and fusses because it wants milk, and in that moment the mother is, above all, the source of what it needs. The Hebrew word David uses, gamul, describes a child who has finished nursing. In ancient Israel, weaning often came late, around two or three years of age. When Abraham's son Isaac was weaned, the family held a great feast (Genesis 21:8), and Hannah kept young Samuel at home until he was weaned before bringing him to serve at the house of the LORD (1 Samuel 1:24). So the child in David's picture is a toddler, old enough to walk and chatter, who climbs into its mother's lap and simply rests there. It comes for her, with nothing to demand.

One way to read this is as a gentle question about our own prayers. Much of the time, we come to God the way a nursing infant comes to its mother: hungry, urgent, reaching for what he can give. God welcomes that, and Scripture freely invites us to bring every request to him (Philippians 4:6). But David describes a deeper kind of closeness, where the soul has learned to be content with God himself. The weaned child still depends on its mother completely. What has changed is that it no longer measures her love by what she places in its hands at that moment. A soul at rest has learned to come to God for God himself, and to find that he is enough.

The verbs carry their own quiet lesson. "I have calmed and quieted myself." The first Hebrew verb, shiwwiti, comes from a root meaning to level or smooth out. The prophet Isaiah uses the same word for a farmer who has "leveled the surface" of his field before sowing (Isaiah 28:25). The second, domamti, means to be silent or still. Together they picture an inner life like a ploughed field, once ridged and rutted, now smoothed and ready. David also says plainly that he did this himself. He speaks of contentment as something he chose and practiced over time, the way a farmer patiently works the same ground season after season.

The psalm that follows shows how hard-won this rest must have been. Psalm 132 opens, "LORD, remember David and all his self-denial" (Psalm 132:1), and then recalls his vow: "I will not enter my house or go to my bed, I will allow no sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, till I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob" (Psalm 132:3–5). David was a man who could not sit still. He longed to give the ark of the covenant (the gold-covered chest that represented God's presence among his people) a worthy home. Yet that same psalm turns to a prayer: "Arise, LORD, and come to your resting place" (Psalm 132:8). The restless king finds his own rest in the place where God chooses to rest.

Scripture is not shy about using a mother's tenderness to describe the Lord. Through Isaiah, God promises his weary people, "As a mother comforts her child, so will I comfort you" (Isaiah 66:13). The lap David climbs into in Psalm 131 belongs to that same God, whose patience with fussing children is far older than our fussing.

Many of us carry great matters that were never ours to carry. We lie awake turning over a test result, a child working abroad, a debt, a decision that belongs to someone else, or a future no one can see yet. We roll these worries over and over in the dark the way an infant fusses for milk. David's little song invites us to sort them gently, asking what is truly ours to do today and what is too wonderful for us and belongs to God. Tonight, before you sleep, you might sit quietly for two minutes with your hands open on your lap, name one worry that is too big for you, and say to the Lord, "This one is yours." Then stay there a moment longer, asking for nothing, the way a child lingers in its mother's arms after the crying has stopped.

The psalm ends by turning outward to the whole people of God: "Israel, put your hope in the LORD both now and forevermore" (Psalm 131:3). One man's quieted heart becomes an invitation for everyone walking up that dusty road, and for us. The babies of Bogotá did not have to understand medicine to grow calm on their mothers' chests; they only had to be held. You do not have to solve tomorrow to rest in God today. Climb into his lap with your worries set down beside you, and let the steady heartbeat of his faithfulness quiet your own.

articles.title: Grabbing the Askal by the Ears
articles.dek: Proverbs gives us one of its funniest pictures for one of our most common habits: rushing into a fight that was never ours. Behind the humor sits a quiet freedom the gospel makes possible.
articles.quote: Jesus already stepped into the one quarrel that was truly yours, so you no longer have to win every quarrel that isn't.
articles.body:
On a weekday afternoon in almost any barangay hall in the Philippines, you can watch a small, unglamorous kind of peace being made. Two neighbors sit on monobloc chairs across a plastic table. One is upset because the other's mango tree drops its leaves into her yard every summer, and the other is upset because she apparently keeps the fruit that falls with them. Between them sits a member of the Lupon Tagapamayapa, the barangay's peace committee, often a retired teacher or a lola who has known both families for thirty years. She keeps her voice low, pours each of them a glass of water, and lets them talk until they run out of words. Then she asks a gentle question that begins with "Paano kung..." ("What if...").

The Katarungang Pambarangay, our village justice system, was set up in 1978 and later written into the Local Government Code of 1991. Most disputes between residents of the same barangay must pass through it before anyone can file a case in court. It is one of the hopeful, underappreciated things about Filipino life: every year, a great many quarrels over fences, small debts, late-night karaoke, and wandering chickens end with a signed agreement and, now and then, a shared merienda. Yet the wisest feature of the Lupon is how its work begins. A complaint is filed, both parties are summoned, and only then does anyone step in. The peacemakers wait to be asked.

Every Filipino also knows the opposite figure. He is the usisero who hears shouting from the next street, leaves his stool outside the sari-sari store, and arrives already taking sides. We even have a word for what he does: makisawsaw, to dip your fingers into someone else's sawsawan. He seldom brings peace, and more often he walks home with a scratch of his own while the original quarrel grows a third side. Proverbs has a picture for him, and once you see it, you will never forget it.

"Like one who grabs a stray dog by the ears is someone who rushes into a quarrel not their own." (Proverbs 26:17)

This proverb comes from a collection that Proverbs 25:1 says was "compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah," royal scribes gathering Solomon's sayings some two centuries after his death so that a new generation could live wisely. Chapter 26 reads like a gallery of difficult people. The first twelve verses describe the fool. Verses 13 to 16 describe the sluggard. From verse 17 onward come the troublemakers of the tongue: the meddler, the prankster who wounds and then says "I was only joking!" (26:19), and the gossip, about whom the writer says, "Without wood a fire goes out; without a gossip a quarrel dies down" (26:20).

The dog in verse 17 matters. In ancient Israel, dogs were rarely pets. They were half-wild scavengers that roamed the edges of town, and the psalmist describes enemies who "return at evening, snarling like dogs, and prowl about the city" (Psalm 59:6). Anyone who has walked past an askal guarding a pile of garbage at night understands the image at once. Grabbing such a dog by the ears is a decision you cannot undo. While you hold on, the dog twists and snaps, and the moment you let go, it turns on the one person within reach, which is you.

The Hebrew sharpens the picture. The verse opens with a word for someone "passing by," a traveler with somewhere else to be. The word the NIV renders "rushes" is mit'abber, from a root meaning "to cross over," and in this form it usually means working oneself into a fury. The same word appears in Proverbs 14:16, where "a fool is hotheaded and yet feels secure." So the man in verse 17 is a passerby who crosses a line twice: he steps into someone else's business, and he lets someone else's anger become his own. The quarrel did not belong to him, but by the time he arrives, the heat certainly does.

One way to read this verse is alongside the sluggard who comes just before it. That man refuses to leave his house for honest work, insisting, "There's a lion in the road, a fierce lion roaming the streets!" (26:13). He imagines danger so that he can avoid what is truly his to do. A few lines later, the meddler ignores real danger to chase what was never his to do. Placed side by side, they suggest that both men have made the same mistake in opposite directions. Each has misjudged what belongs to him. Wisdom, in the eyes of Proverbs, includes knowing the borders of your own assignment, so that you are brave about your own road and humble about everyone else's.

None of this means Christians should look away from conflict. Jesus said, "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God" (Matthew 5:9), and Paul told believers that when someone stumbles, "you who live by the Spirit should restore that person gently" (Galatians 6:1). The difference lies in the posture. The peacemaker arrives slowly, calmly, and usually by invitation, like the lola at the barangay table. The meddler arrives fast, hot, and uninvited. Even Jesus, when a man in the crowd demanded, "Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me," answered, "Man, who appointed me a judge or an arbiter between you?" (Luke 12:13–14). He then spoke to the heart of the matter, warning the man about greed, and left the family dispute where it belonged.

Here the gospel makes all of this beautiful. There was one quarrel Jesus did walk into, deliberately and at great cost: the long estrangement between a holy God and rebellious people. Paul writes that "while we were God's enemies, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10), and that "there is one God and one mediator between God and mankind, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5). He was sent by the Father, which means the quarrel was given to him. He came without hot temper, and when the bite came, he took it in his own body on the cross. Jesus already stepped into the one quarrel that was truly yours, so you no longer have to win every quarrel that isn't.

That freedom changes ordinary days. Much of our meddling grows from a restless need to be right, to be needed, or to be on the winning side. A heart at peace with God can afford to let some arguments pass by. It can watch the family group chat catch fire over an old inheritance issue, or a Facebook thread turn ugly over a neighbor's parking, and choose a quieter path. Sometimes that path is silence, and sometimes it is a private, gentle message to each person you love, sent a day later when tempers have cooled. Very often it begins with praying for both of them by name before you say anything at all.

Before you step into the next conflict around you, it helps to ask yourself two honest questions: "Was I asked, or am I simply curious?" and "Am I calm, or has their anger already become mine?" If the answers are no and no, you may well be reaching for the ears of a stray dog. If someone has asked for your help and your heart is quiet, then go, slowly and kindly, the way the Lupon lola pours the water before she says a word.

May today find you less eager to win and more ready to bless. Christ has already made peace on your behalf, and his peace in you can do something no usisero ever managed. It can help a quarrel die down, the way a fire goes out when someone simply stops adding wood.
